title: Selective Control and Imaging of Higgs and Goldstone Modes with a Quantum Simulator
authors: Connie Miao, Pranjal Praneel, Thomas G. Kiely, Eliott Rosenberg, Nicole S. Ticea, Pedram Roushan, Erich Mueller, Andre G. Petukhov
abstract: We realize the mesoscopic Bose-Hubbard model at unit-filling on a two-dimensional array of transmon qubits and selectively excite collective modes associated with amplitude or phase fluctuations of the superfluid order parameter. We identify these modes respectively as the Higgs and Goldstone modes using complementary local observables, extracted from measuring the number of particles on each site. Modulation of the coupling between sites excites the Higgs mode, which we detect via the density of doubly occupied sites. In contrast, modulation of the local chemical potential with an appropriately chosen spatial profile excites the lowest-frequency Goldstone mode, which we detect via changes in the local density. The two modes have different symmetries and do not couple to one another. By varying the system geometry, we characterize the impact of finite system size on the evolution of both modes. In the thermodynamic limit, decay into a continuum of lower-energy excitations can obscure the Higgs response. In our mesoscopic system, however, the finite system size leads to spectral gaps and allows us to detect the Higgs mode as a coherent, long-lived excitation. Our work demonstrates how finite quantum simulators can isolate and probe physical phenomena that become difficult to resolve in the thermodynamic, large-scale limit.
summary: This paper reports on the selective control and imaging of Higgs and Goldstone collective modes in a Bose-Hubbard model simulated using transmon qubits. By using complementary local observables, the authors distinguish between amplitude (Higgs) and phase (Goldstone) fluctuations. Crucially, they show that the finite size of the quantum simulator allows for the coherent detection of the Higgs mode, a feature obscured in the idealized thermodynamic limit.
main_problem: The study aims to selectively control and image the dynamics of Higgs and Goldstone collective modes associated with amplitude and phase fluctuations in a lattice superfluid.
main_result: The research successfully demonstrates that finite quantum simulators can isolate and coherently probe the Higgs mode, overcoming spectral decay issues present in the thermodynamic limit.
method: The study combines experimental techniques like vacuum Rabi spectroscopy and drive spectroscopy with theoretical tools like Matrix Product States (MPS) ansatzes for spectral function calculations.
model_or_system: The system is modeled by the Bose-Hubbard Hamiltonian, realized experimentally on a two-dimensional array of transmon qubits, operating in the unit-filling regime.
key_observables: Doublon fraction oscillations, local density fluctuations, and the spectral function $S(\omega)$ are used to diagnose the modes.
important_parameters: The hopping strength ($J$), on-site interaction ($U$), and the ratio $J/U$ are key parameters, with finite system size effects being crucial.
main_assumptions: The detection of the Higgs mode relies on the finite system size creating spectral gaps, and the analysis assumes the validity of the amplitude/phase mode picture.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the free-energy landscape and the distinct signatures of Goldstone (density waves) and Higgs (doublon-holon pair oscillations) modes, alongside spectroscopy results mapping spectra across the phase transition.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the physical model and Hamiltonian, detailing the separate excitation protocols for the Higgs and Goldstone modes, presenting measurements showing mode selectivity, and finally discussing finite-size scaling relative to the thermodynamic limit.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, experimentally realized platform (qubits) to study fundamental concepts of symmetry breaking and collective excitations (Higgs/Goldstone) in quantum many-body systems, bridging theory and cutting-edge quantum hardware.
